subsection: 4. Irish nationalism and Ulster Unionism as international forces

notes.h: Background: why Ireland had a diaspora
notes.b: Irish nationalism and Ulster Unionism both looked abroad for help because millions of Irish people, and their descendants, lived outside Ireland. The background below is what the later events rest on.
points: The Famine (1845 to 1852) and the mass emigration that followed created large Irish communities in the United States, Britain, Canada and Australia, and many emigrants carried bitter memories of British rule, which made them willing to fund nationalist causes.

Home Rule (a self-governing parliament for Ireland within the United Kingdom) was pursued by the Irish Parliamentary Party. The Home Rule crisis of 1912 to 1914 pitted Ulster Unionists, who armed themselves in the Ulster Volunteer Force, against it.
The Rising of 1916, the War of Independence and the Treaty of 1921 form the Irish setting for American and other overseas support for republicans.
Many Ulster Presbyterians emigrated to North America in the eighteenth century, and their descendants kept a sense of Ulster origins, which later gave Unionists an overseas audience.
The Orange Order is a Protestant fraternal society (a brotherhood with its own lodges and rituals), and it had lodges overseas as well as in Ulster, so it gave Unionists a ready-made network abroad.

notes.h: Fenianism and Irish America, 1858 to the 1880s
notes.b: Irish nationalism became an international force through emigrant organisations in the United States, Canada and Britain, which raised money and planned rebellion. Emigrants who could not change Ireland by voting at home could pay for those who would fight.
points: The Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB) was founded in Dublin on 17 March 1858 by James Stephens. It aimed at an independent Irish republic won by armed force, because Fenians believed Britain would never give up Ireland peacefully.

The Fenian Brotherhood was founded in New York in 1858 by John O'Mahony as the American wing of the movement. It drew on Irish emigrants and on veterans of the American Civil War, who had military training.
Fenian money came from Irish emigrant workers in American cities and paid for preparations for the Irish rising of 1867, which failed.

In June 1866 Fenians crossed the Niagara River into Canada and won a skirmish at Ridgeway, Ontario, before withdrawing. The US authorities arrested some of them and pressed the Fenians to stop, so the raid achieved nothing for Ireland.
The raids failed, and they are generally said to have helped Canadian confederation (1867) by alarming the Canadian colonies. A further raid in 1870 was defeated.
Clan na Gael was founded in New York in 1867 as a secret republican society for Irish Americans. As the Fenian Brotherhood declined it became the strongest republican body in the United States.

The Hougoumont, the last convict ship to Australia, carried about 60 Fenian prisoners to Western Australia in 1867 to 1868 (arriving in January 1868). Irish-American opinion supported campaigns for the release of imprisoned Fenians.

Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa's Skirmishing Fund, launched in New York in 1876, paid for the dynamite campaign in English cities in the early to mid 1880s. This extended the use of American money to pay for violence.
notes.tip: Keep the three bodies apart: the IRB was in Ireland (Stephens, 1858), the Fenian Brotherhood in America (O'Mahony, 1858), and Clan na Gael in America (1867), the later and stronger body. Do not confuse the Hougoumont (1867 to 1868, transport of convicts) with the Catalpa (1876, a rescue). If asked why Clan na Gael became the main American body, say that the Fenian Brotherhood declined.

notes.b: John Devoy was the most important Irish-American republican of his generation, and his career links the Fenians of the 1860s with the Rising of 1916. The first half of his story runs from Ireland to exile and the Catalpa.
points: John Devoy was born in Co. Kildare in 1842 and joined the IRB in the 1860s, where he recruited Fenians among Irish soldiers in the British Army.

He was arrested in 1866 and sentenced to 15 years' penal servitude for treason-felony (the charge of plotting against the Crown). He was released in 1871 on condition of exile and sailed to New York on the Cuba with other prisoners.
In America he became a leading figure in Clan na Gael and used Irish-American newspapers to argue for an independent Irish republic, because newspapers reached emigrants across many cities.
In 1876 Devoy and Clan na Gael organised the Catalpa rescue, in which the American whaler Catalpa freed six Fenian prisoners from Western Australia.

In 1878 he proposed the New Departure with Michael Davitt. This was a plan for Fenians to cooperate with Charles Stewart Parnell's constitutional nationalists (those who sought change through Parliament) on land reform and self-government.
He founded the Gaelic American newspaper in New York in 1903 and edited it, so that he could keep Irish-American opinion behind the republican cause.
notes.tip: For a short answer on Devoy, give a chain of dated facts: born 1842, Fenian, arrested 1866, exile 1871, Catalpa 1876, New Departure 1878, Gaelic American 1903, support for the Rising in 1916. Each correct dated statement earns marks.

notes.h: Key personality: John Devoy, 1914 to 1928 and how he is judged
notes.b: Devoy's last great effort was to help bring about the Rising of 1916, and his later life was darkened by a quarrel with the new republican leadership.
points: In 1914 he and Judge Daniel Cohalan met the German ambassador in Washington, Count Bernstorff, to ask for German help for a rising. Clan na Gael also sent money to the IRB before the Rising of 1916.
After 1919 he quarrelled bitterly with de Valera, the republican leader, yet he supported the Treaty of 1921. He visited the Irish Free State in 1924 and died in 1928.

Contemporaries judged him differently: British opinion regarded him as a dangerous revolutionary, many Irish Americans saw him as an elder statesman of the republican cause, and de Valera's supporters saw him as an obstinate old man.

Historians such as Terry Golway, in his biography Irish Rebel (1998), present him as a central link between Fenian conspiracy in Ireland and organised Irish-American support for republicanism in the twentieth century. His memoir Recollections of an Irish Rebel was published in 1929.
notes.tip: A strong essay on Devoy names how contemporaries and historians judged him. Naming Golway adds weight.

notes.h: Land League, Parnell and Davitt in America
notes.b: Irish nationalists raised money in America for the land agitation of 1879 to 1882, and American support gave the movement a wide base. The campaign was about land: tenants wanted lower rents and protection from landlords.
points: Michael Davitt, a Fenian released from prison in 1877, visited America in 1878. His work with Devoy produced the New Departure of 1878, which linked physical-force republicans with constitutional nationalists and the land question.
The Irish National Land League was founded in 1879, with Parnell as president and Davitt as a founder. It campaigned against rack-renting (charging tenants excessive rents) and eviction.
Parnell toured the United States in early 1880, raising funds among Irish Americans and addressing the House of Representatives in Washington.
Patrick Ford's newspaper the Irish World raised money for the Land League and for evicted tenants, because its readers were Irish emigrants who sympathised with them.
The American Ladies' Land League was founded in New York in 1880 and led by Fanny Parnell. The Land League itself was suppressed in 1881.
American money paid for relief to evicted tenants and sustained the League's campaign, which made American money a direct force in Irish agrarian politics.
notes.tip: If asked why American money mattered to the Land League, say that it relieved evicted tenants and kept the campaign going. Do not give any sums, since none are firmly known. Remember that Devoy was the republican, Davitt the Land League founder and Parnell the constitutional leader, and that the New Departure joined all three strands.

notes.h: Irish nationalism in Britain and Australia
notes.b: Irish nationalist organisations in Britain and Australia gave the movement support beyond the United States, though their influence was smaller.
points: The Irish National League of Great Britain, founded in 1883, organised Irish voters in Liverpool, Glasgow and other British cities behind the Irish Parliamentary Party.
The Irish Self-Determination League of Great Britain, founded in 1919, campaigned for the Irish Republic among Irish emigrants in Britain during the War of Independence.

Irish Catholic communities in Australia supported Home Rule through their churches and press, so priests and newspapers spread the cause. John and William Redmond toured Australia in 1883 to raise funds for the cause.
After 1916 Irish Australians, led by Archbishop Mannix, opposed conscription (compulsory military service) and supported Irish independence.
The Fenian prisoners transported to Western Australia and the Catalpa rescue gave Australia a place in Fenian memory, for example through the story of the Hougoumont.

notes.h: Irish America and the Rising of 1916
notes.b: Irish-American organisations gave money and support to the 1916 Rising, and their divisions shaped Irish politics after 1918.
points: Clan na Gael supported the Rising with money and contacts, and Devoy and Cohalan sought German help through contact with the German ambassador in Washington.
The Irish Race Convention held in New York in March 1916 launched the Friends of Irish Freedom, led by Judge Daniel Cohalan and Devoy.
The Aud, a German arms ship sent for the Rising, was intercepted by the Royal Navy and scuttled off Cork in April 1916, so the weapons never reached the rebels.
After the Rising and the executions of its leaders, Irish-American opinion moved strongly behind the Irish Republic, and the Friends of Irish Freedom raised money and lobbied Congress.

An Irish Race Convention in Philadelphia in February 1919 appealed to the Paris Peace Conference and President Wilson to support Irish self-determination (the right of a people to choose its own government).
Divisions among Irish-American leaders, especially between Devoy and Cohalan on one side and Éamon de Valera on the other, weakened the unity of the movement after 1919.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Irish Race Convention of 1916 (New York, which launched the Friends of Irish Freedom) with that of 1919 (Philadelphia). The Friends of Irish Freedom (1916) is a different body from the Fenian Brotherhood (1858).

notes.b: After the partition of Ireland, nationalists sought international support against the border, and Irish America was a key source of lobbying. The campaign achieved no change.
points: The Government of Ireland Act of 1920 created Northern Ireland. The border with the Irish Free State was confirmed when the Boundary Commission collapsed in 1925.
The Anti-Partition League was formed in 1945 to unite nationalists, so that they could speak with one voice, and it sought support in Ireland, Britain and America.
Éamon de Valera, then leader of the opposition, toured the USA and other countries in 1948 to press the anti-partition case, but no US government action followed.
In September 1948 Taoiseach John A. Costello announced in Ottawa the intention to repeal the External Relations Act, and the Republic of Ireland Act came into force on 18 April 1949.
Britain answered with the Ireland Act of 1949, which guaranteed that Northern Ireland would remain in the United Kingdom unless its parliament decided otherwise.
Ireland declined to join NATO in 1949 because of partition, and Seán MacBride, as Minister for External Affairs, appealed to American politicians and press.
Congressman John Fogarty of Rhode Island proposed in 1950 that American aid to Britain be linked to ending partition. The proposal failed.
notes.tip: If asked why the campaign failed, give no US government action, Britain's Ireland Act and the Irish government's weakness abroad. Keep three dates apart: Costello's Ottawa announcement (1948), the Republic of Ireland Act (in force 1949) and Britain's Ireland Act (1949).

notes.b: Ulster Unionists looked for support among emigrants of Ulster Protestant descent in North America and the Dominions (self-governing countries of the British Empire), and their appeal rested on a shared Ulster-Scots identity.
points: Ulster-Scots (or Scotch-Irish) identity means descent from Ulster Presbyterian settlers. In the United States and Canada these descendants kept a sense of Ulster origins, and a Scotch-Irish Society of America held its first congress in 1889.
Andrew Jackson and Woodrow Wilson, two US presidents, were of Ulster-Scots descent, which Unionists could point to as proof of the Ulster connection with America.

The Ulster Covenant of 28 September 1912 was signed by nearly half a million men and women (men signed the Covenant and women a parallel declaration) to oppose Home Rule, and it became the symbol of loyalist resistance that was publicised abroad.

The Orange Order, founded in Co. Armagh in 1795, had strong lodges in Canada, in Ontario and Toronto. They were politically significant and gave moral support to Ulster Unionism during the Home Rule crisis.
In Australia, Orange lodges in Victoria and New South Wales supported the British connection and opposed Home Rule for Ireland.

Unionist lobbying abroad relied on Scotch-Irish and Orange networks. It had moral and some financial value but little influence on British policy, which makes it far smaller in scale than the nationalist networks.
notes.tip: Credit goes to answers that say Unionist influence abroad was moral rather than decisive. A comparison with the nationalist networks, which were larger and funded and armed a movement, earns more.

notes.b: Bonar Law was born in Canada to an Ulster Presbyterian father, and he led the Conservatives in the Home Rule crisis before becoming Prime Minister in 1922. He was Canadian-born but of Ulster descent, and he was not himself an emigrant organiser.
points: Andrew Bonar Law was born in 1858 at Kingston, New Brunswick, the son of the Rev. James Law, an Ulster Presbyterian minister.
The family moved to Glasgow in 1870, and Bonar Law went into the iron trade there before entering Parliament in 1900.
He became leader of the Conservative Party in November 1911, succeeding Arthur Balfour, which put a Unionist sympathiser at the head of the opposition.
At Blenheim Palace in July 1912, he said he could imagine no length of resistance to which Ulster could go that he would not support. This was two months before the Ulster Covenant.
He was a leading Unionist in the Home Rule crisis of 1912 to 1914, and his support for the Ulster Unionists made the exclusion of Ulster a Conservative aim.

He served in the wartime coalition and was Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1916 to 1919 in Lloyd George's coalition. He became Prime Minister in October 1922, resigned in May 1923 because of cancer and died in October 1923.
Contemporary opinion was divided: Liberal and nationalist newspapers portrayed him as a reckless partisan, while unionists praised him as a loyal champion.
Historians such as Robert Blake (The Unknown Prime Minister, 1955) stress his role in shaping Conservative policy on Ulster, and they debate how far his stand made partition more likely.
notes.tip: Give at least three dated actions: Conservative leadership in 1911, Blenheim in July 1912 and Prime Minister in 1922. Do not mix up the Blenheim speech (July 1912) with the Ulster Covenant (September 1912), which were different events.

notes.h: Assessment: nationalist and unionist networks abroad
notes.b: Examiners reward a clear judgement stated early and balanced with named achievements and limits. The general pattern is that diaspora support sustained movements but rarely decided outcomes.
points: Achievement: Fenian and Clan na Gael networks funded and armed the nationalist movement, Land League funds sustained the agitation of 1879 to 1882, and Irish America shaped events from 1916 to 1919.
Limit: the Fenian rising of 1867 and the raids into Canada failed, and the quarrel between Devoy and Cohalan on one side and de Valera on the other weakened support in America.
Anti-partition campaigners won sympathy in America after 1945 but failed to end partition.
Unionist networks won real sympathy through Orange and Scotch-Irish links, but they had little effect on British policy, and they were small beside the nationalist networks.
Contemporary view: British officials regarded Irish-American networks as threats to security, while Irish-American leaders saw themselves as allies of the Irish cause.
Later view: historians debate whether diaspora money or politics in Ireland and Britain decided events, and many stress that the decisive events happened in Ireland and Britain.
notes.tip: In the 100-mark essay, state your verdict at the start, balance achievements against limits with named organisations and dates, and compare nationalist and unionist networks directly. Separate money, organisation and publicity from actual results.
